companies.foundedNote: Jeff Bezos filed articles of incorporation in Washington State on 1994-07-05 under the name Cadabra, Inc., and renamed it Amazon.com, Inc. within a few months after a lawyer misheard 'Cadabra' as 'cadaver'. The filings corroborate the month but not the day: the IPO prospectus says only 'The Company was incorporated in Washington in July 1994', and records Bezos buying 10,200,000 founder shares for $10,000 in July 1994. The 1994-07-05 date and the Cadabra name come from Wikipedia rather than from a filing. Amazon reincorporated in Delaware on 1996-05-28 through a Washington-into-Delaware merger (S-1 Exhibit 2.1, 'Agreement and Plan of Merger dated May 28, 1996'), five weeks before the Kleiner Perkins round; per the brief this chart clocks from the original Washington incorporation, so t=0 is 22 months before the Delaware entity existed.

notes.0: First round with a named institutional lead, and the only pre-IPO institutional round. Reconstructed from the legal cap table rather than from press: the prospectus records 555,161 shares to Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers VIII and 14,235 to KPCB Information Sciences Zaibatsu Fund II, both at $14.05 per share — 569,396 shares for $8,000,013.80. S-1 Exhibit 10.2, the Series A Preferred Stock Purchase Agreement dated June 21, 1996, gives the closing-day denominator in its section 2.2 capitalisation representation: 2,589,711 common shares issued and outstanding. Series A converted 1:1 at the time (6:1 after the November 1996 4-for-1 and April 1997 3-for-2 splits), so post-money on outstanding as-converted shares is (2,589,711 + 569,396) x $14.05 = $44.39M, pre-money $36.39M, and Kleiner's stake 18.0% — which the prospectus corroborates at 16.3% by May 1997 after a year of dilution. The widely repeated '$8M for 13% at a $60M valuation' (HistoryLink, following Brad Stone) cannot be reconciled with those share counts: 13% would require 4.38M shares outstanding when the signed agreement says 3.16M. Adding the 414,636 options then outstanding and the 341,615-share reserve gets to $55.0M fully diluted, which is the closest any defensible convention comes to $60M. Marked soft because the choice between the outstanding and fully-diluted convention moves the number 24%.

unresolved: The 1995-96 angel syndicate: the S-1 equity statement implies ~2.8M shares at $0.3333 beyond the family purchases, but the per-share arithmetic does not close against the rounded $1,172,000 total, and no filing names the investors.

Whether the widely cited '$8M for 13% at $60M' for the June 1996 round reflects some fully-diluted convention or is simply wrong. The signed purchase agreement's share counts support 18.0% and $44.4M outstanding, or $55.0M fully diluted; neither yields 13%.

First, an angel syndicate: the statement of stockholders' equity shows 4,235,244 common shares sold during 1995 for $1,172,000, of which only 1,430,244 shares / $245,573 were the family purchases, leaving roughly 2.8M shares at $0.3333 — the ~$1M raised from about twenty angels that secondary accounts describe, including director Tom A. The prospectus body says only 'We were incorporated in Delaware in February 1999' and 'We were founded in February 1999'; the exhibit supplies the day, which is exactly the case RESEARCH.md makes for reading the exhibits. Popular accounts date the founding to March 1999, when Marc Benioff, Parker Harris, Dave Moellenhoff and Frank Dominguez started work in a rented apartment on Telegraph Hill in San Francisco; that is a team-founding date a month after the charter. This chart clocks from the earliest formal founding, so t=0 is the Delaware filing.

notes.0: 10,000,000 shares at $11.00. The final prospectus states 101,256,880 shares of common stock outstanding after the offering, which at the offer price is $1,113,825,680 — Salesforce crossed a billion dollars on its first day, five years and four months after incorporation. All 58,024,345 preferred shares converted at closing.

unresolved: Post-money valuation for all four pre-IPO rounds. Price per share is known for each; no filing gives the fully-diluted count at any closing.
Larry Ellison's reported $2,000,000 seed investment — real by every secondary account, but absent from the S-1's preferred-sales table and therefore not recorded as a fact here.

companies.curatorNotes: Salesforce is the clearest illustration in this dataset of why the inclusion floor is a mechanical test rather than a series letter. Its Series A, B and C — three rounds and $17.5 million across 1999 — were funded almost entirely by Marc Benioff himself, Halsey Minor, Magdalena Yesil and other individuals, with no venture capital firm named in any of them; the first round with institutional funds in it is the Series D, and a reader going by letters alone would have started the line two years early. Every share count, price and date here comes from the S-1's related-party table and Item 15, cross-read against Exhibit 3.1's authorised-share schedule (25,850,000 Series A, 12,588,345 Series B, 7,650,498 Series C), which independently confirms the A and B counts. None of the four rounds discloses a post-money and none is reconstructible, so none is plotted; the line starts at the IPO. Total pre-IPO capital raised was $64,376,034. One split, 4:1 in April 2013, which the pipeline derives from the cover-page share series. Salesforce's fiscal year ends January 31, so its 10-K and 10-Q cover dates sit at odd-looking points in the calendar (the share count used for the 2025-12-31 checkpoint below is dated 2025-11-28, from the Q3 FY2026 10-Q); the chart itself is on calendar quarters throughout and is unaffected.

companies.name: SpaceX
companies.foundedNote: The IPO prospectus states it twice. The business section says 'We were founded and incorporated as Space Exploration Technologies Corp., a Delaware corporation, on March 14, 2002 and reincorporated as a Texas corporation on February 14, 2024', and Note 1 says 'SpaceX was incorporated in the state of Delaware on March 14, 2002 and converted into a corporation organized under the laws of the State of Texas on February 14, 2024.' No earlier partnership exists, and the 2024 Texas conversion is a change of domicile, not a new founding, so the original Delaware incorporation is used. The widely repeated date of 2002-05-06 is a de facto team-founding date: Wikipedia's History of SpaceX says the 'de facto founding date might instead be May 6' or around June, while 'According to filings, SpaceX was incorporated on March 14, 2002'. Later anchors from S-1 Exhibit 4.2: Musk's founding Class B shares were issued 2002-07-08 and the Series A purchase agreement is dated 2002-08-05.

leads.3: Undisclosed (Baillie Gifford named as a participant)
leads.6: Undisclosed (Bloomberg reported Fidelity among the largest participants, unconfirmed)

notes.0: Form D date of first sale 2015-01-20: $999,999,925 sold from 13 investors (the Series G purchase agreement is dated 2015-01-16). S-1: $77.46 issue price, 12.6M shares still outstanding. Reuters (via Fortune) says only that Google and Fidelity together hold 'just under 10%'; Donald Harrison of Google joined the board in February 2015. The valuation conflicts across outlets: Wikipedia, citing the WSJ, gives 8.33% for $1B, about $12B. The FT, relayed by Global Venturing, said 'more than $10bn'. CNBC (2017) said 'around $11 billion' and Fortune (2018) said $10B. The highest well-sourced figure, $12B, is used and the others are rejected here. SpaceX never confirmed a valuation, and the WSJ piece itself was not loaded, so this is soft.
notes.1: Form D date of first sale 2017-07-26. The D/A shows the offering grew from $351M to $449,999,820, from 25 investors, which divides into exactly 3,333,332 shares at the S-1's $135.00 Series H price. CNBC (2017-07-27) reported 'up to $350 million' with SpaceX 'now valued at around $21 billion', from filings obtained by Equidate. Fortune (2018) cites PitchBook's $20.8B for the completed $450M. The two figures are close; the higher, $21B, is used and $20.8B is rejected here. No lead was reported.
notes.2: Form D date of first sale 2018-04-05: $214,000,137 sold at filing (exactly 1,266,273 shares at $169) of a $500,000,189 offering. The amount used is the larger documented floor, the S-1's $499M Series I liquidation preference (3.0M shares at $169.00). The valuation conflicts: Reuters (2018-04-12), from the filing, says 'around $26 billion' and notes the $169 price was 25% above the prior round. Fortune and Bloomberg, both citing PitchBook (so one source), say $25B. The higher, $26B, is used and $25B is rejected here. No lead was reported.
notes.3: Form D date of first sale 2018-12-21. The D/A total of $486,198,978 from 8 investors is exactly 2,613,973 shares at the S-1's $186.00 Series J price. Fortune (2018-12-18), relaying the WSJ, gives the $30.5B valuation and names Baillie Gifford among the investors, without a lead. CNBC (2019-05-31) repeats 'valued at $30.5 billion'. Exhibit 4.2 separately carves out Fidelity's and Baillie Gifford's right to disclose their holdings. Soft, because both outlets trace to the same WSJ report and SpaceX never confirmed.
notes.4: Form D date of first sale 2019-04-08. The D/A total of $535,744,188 from 5 investors is exactly 2,626,197 shares at the S-1's $204.00 Series K price. CNBC (2019-05-31): 'the company's latest round brought in $536 million at a price of $204 a share' and the value 'has risen to $33.3 billion', from people familiar with the fundraising. Single outlet, anonymous sourcing.
notes.5: Form D date of first sale 2020-02-28. The D/A reports $346,224,340 sold (exactly 1,573,747 shares at $220), and CNBC (2020-05-26) reports the same $346.2M at 'a valuation of around $36 billion'. CNBC (2020-03-09) had reported $500.06M authorized at $220 a share, valuing SpaceX at around $36B. The S-1 shows 2.7M Series M shares outstanding, a $596M liquidation preference, so about $250M more was sold after the last Form D amendment; the S-1 figure is used. Single outlet.
notes.6: Form D date of first sale 2020-08-04 (also the Series N purchase-agreement date): $1,901,446,920 sold at filing (exactly 7,042,396 shares at $270) from 75 investors, of a $2,066,446,620 offering. TechCrunch (2020-08-18) says Bloomberg 'pegged the post-money valuation of SpaceX at $46 billion following this raise', and CNBC (2021-02-16) independently describes the round as 'near $2 billion at a $46 billion valuation'. An October 2020 CNBC mention of $44B is the rejected lower figure. Soft, because SpaceX never confirmed.
notes.7: Form D date of first sale 2021-02-16; the April 2021 D/A raised the total to $1,164,061,924 from 99 investors. It is the first raise after Series N and created no new preferred series. CNBC (2021-02-16): $850M 'at $419.99 a share', 'sending the company's valuation skyrocketing to about $74 billion', with a concurrent $750M insider secondary at the same terms. CNBC (2021-04-14) confirms the second close to $1.16B. Wikipedia's '$1.61 billion from 99 investors' is a transposition of the filed $1.16B. Single outlet, anonymous sourcing.
notes.8: Company-arranged secondary: CNBC (2021-10-08) reports 'an agreement with new and existing investors' to 'sell up to $755 million in stock from insiders at $560 a share', 'increasing the company's valuation to $100.3 billion'. No new capital was raised, so amountRaisedUsd is null and $755M is the offer ceiling. Secondary price, soft. Date is the report date; closing was not disclosed.
notes.9: Form D date of first sale 2022-05-27; the D/A shows $1,724,965,480 fully sold from 74 investors, exactly 24,642,364 shares at $70. The $70 is post the February 2022 10-for-1 split ($700 on the old basis). Single outlet, but based on a company document.
notes.10: SpaceX filed no Form D after July 2022, so every later private-market transaction was a sale of existing shares. CNBC (2023-01-02) reported a $750M deal that 'values the company at $137 billion', with Andreessen Horowitz 'likely' to lead per an email to prospective investors. It cites Bloomberg's report that SpaceX was 'allowing insiders to sell at $77 per share'. Fortune (2026) confirms a16z first backed SpaceX in 2023 'when the company was still valued at $137 billion'. Date is the CNBC report date. Secondary price, soft.
notes.11: CNBC (2023-07-13): a purchase offer 'sent by CFO Bret Johnsen' to sell 'up to $750 million in stock from insiders' at '$81 a share', putting the valuation 'near $150 billion'. No new capital. Secondary price, soft.
notes.12: CNBC (2023-12-13) confirmed the valuation 'hit $180 billion based on an ongoing secondary share sale' at '$97 a share', 'expected to close in January'. Reuters, relaying Bloomberg, says the price rose from about $95 to $97 and puts the size at $500M-$750M. No new capital. Two outlets agree, but a tender price is soft by method.
notes.13: Bloomberg (2024-06-26, via Yahoo Finance): SpaceX 'will sell insider shares at $112 apiece in a tender offer', lifting its value 'closer to $210 billion'; terms not final. CNBC (2024-12-11) later refers to the $210B 'reached in a June 2024 secondary sale'. Secondary price, soft.
notes.14: CNBC (2024-12-11): a $1.25B purchase offer at '$185 a share' values SpaceX at $350B, with SpaceX itself buying up to $500M ('a rare share buyback') alongside investors, and 'no new capital'. The S-1 records $920M of common-stock repurchases from employees and holders in 2024. Bloomberg first reported the pricing. Secondary price, soft.
notes.15: Bloomberg (via the Spokesman-Review, 2025-07-15): a share sale at '$212' a share 'would value the company at about $400 billion', with SpaceX repurchasing up to $1.25B from employees and other holders. The S-1 independently corroborates the price: the October 2025 409A option strike and the September 2025 EchoStar share consideration are both $42.40, which is $212 on the pre-May-2026 basis (5-for-1 split). S-1: $522M of common repurchased in 2025. Date is the report date. Secondary price, soft.
notes.16: Reuters (via CNBC, 2025-12-13) read CFO Bret Johnsen's shareholder letter 'dated Dec. 12': 'new and existing investors and the company will buy up to $2.56 billion of shares from eligible shareholders at $421 a share', valuing SpaceX at $800B. Bloomberg and the NYT also reported it. Dated to the letter. Company-run, so plotted, but a secondary price, so soft.
notes.17: THE FIGURE IS THE OFFERING PRICE x POST-OFFERING SHARES, NOT THE FIRST-DAY CLOSE. The 424B4 (dated 2026-06-11) prices 555,555,555 Class A shares at a fixed $135.00, with an 83,333,333-share over-allotment. The Q2 10-Q confirms the option was exercised in full at the 2026-06-15 closing: 638,888,888 shares for $86,249,999,880 gross ($85,675M net). Shares outstanding after the offering with full exercise, per the 424B4, are 7,463,530,243 Class A plus 5,695,668,265 Class B = 13,159,198,508, x $135 = $1,776,491,798,580. The base case without the option is $1,765,241,798,625, the '$1.77 trillion' CNBC and Wikipedia report. The count includes 1,302,072,285 unvested performance-restricted Class B shares granted to Musk in 2026; without them the offering value is ~$1.60T. Pricing was 2026-06-11 and trading opened 2026-06-12 at $150. CNBC reports a first close of $160.95, valuing SpaceX at $2.1T. That close is left to the pipeline's public series, as plotting it here would assert SpaceX sold stock at that price.

companies.curatorNotes: SOURCING. The S-1 preferred-stock note (424B4 Note 13) lists every SpaceX series, A through N, with original issue price and shares outstanding. S-1 Exhibit 4.2 dates each series' purchase agreement (A 2002-08-05, B 2005-02-24, C 2007-02-28, D 2008-07-21, E 2009-03-18, F 2010-10-28, G 2015-01-16, H 2017-07-26, I 2018-04-05, J 2018-12-21, K 2019-04-08, L 2019-06-24, M 2020-02-28, N 2020-08-04). The electronic Form Ds (2009 onward) match those dates, and every Form D total from 2017 on divides into a whole share count at the matching S-1 series price. That pins the series-to-round mapping without relying on press labels. AMOUNTS use the larger of two documented floors: the Form D total sold (as of filing) and the S-1 liquidation preference of the shares still outstanding at 2025-12-31 (net of buybacks). Series M and N closed roughly $250M and $620M beyond their last Form D amendments. PER-SHARE BASIS: S-1 issue prices are pre-split. Common split 10-for-1 in February 2022 and 5-for-1 on 2026-05-04, and each preferred share converted into 50 Class A or B shares at the IPO. Press prices before 2022 ($419.99, $560) are on the oldest basis, 2022-2025 prices ($70-$421) on the middle basis, and the $135 IPO price on today's basis. VALUATIONS: none was ever company-confirmed before the IPO, so every private figure is soft. The pre-2015 rounds (Founders Fund, DFJ, Series F) never had a post-money reported, so the plotted line starts in 2015, 13 years after founding, and the gap is honest. WHAT THE SCHEMA CANNOT HOLD: (1) The xAI merger, effective 2026-02-02, was an all-stock share exchange, not a priced round or tender. Wikipedia reports it valued SpaceX at $1T and xAI at $250B ($1.25T combined). The S-1 gives the mechanics: 0.1433 SpaceX shares or $75.46 cash per xAI share (pre-split), which implies about $526.59 per SpaceX share pre-split ($105.32 post-split); that is my arithmetic, not a filed figure. The S-1 shows SpaceX repurchasing shares after 2026-03-31 at a weighted-average $105.32, which corroborates it. The merger is excluded from events because no event kind fits, but it is the only private mark between the $800B December 2025 tender and the IPO. (2) Cursor (Anysphere) was acquired after the IPO under a 2026-06-16 merger agreement at a $60.0B implied equity value. It closed 2026-08-14 for 391,041,680 Class A shares (389,289,254 for equity plus 1,752,426 for vested RSUs, per the 8-K). It is not a valuation event for SpaceX, but it is why the cover-page share count rises between Q2 and Q3 2026. (3) The EchoStar spectrum purchase (261.8M Class A shares at $42.40) had not closed at the IPO and is excluded from the offering share count. PUBLIC SERIES: SpaceX has two share classes, so its dei:EntityCommonStockSharesOutstanding is dimensional and absent from the companyfacts API. The only non-dimensional share tag, WeightedAverageNumberOfSharesOutstandingBasic, has just 4 quarterly rows (Q2/Q3 2025, Q2/Q3 2026), under the pipeline's 8-row minimum. That tag would also understate cap by about 12%, because it excludes Musk's ~1.3B unvested restricted Class B shares, which the aggregators include. So until enough 10-Qs accumulate, the pipeline cannot compute quarterly caps and falls back to companiesmarketcap's single 2026 row. REGRESSION: hand computation from filed figures, Q3 2026 10-Q cover (2026-10-15): 8,246,541,218 Class A + 5,334,522,491 Class B = 13,581,063,709 shares, x the stockanalysis 2026-09-30 close of $150.86 = $2.0488T. The same count x the 2026-11-06 close of $134.27 gives $1.8235T, which matches companiesmarketcap's $1.823T exactly, so the aggregators use the full two-class cover count.

companies.name: Palantir
companies.foundedNote: Palantir's S-1 states flatly that the company "was incorporated in Delaware on May 6, 2003." Founded by Peter Thiel, Alex Karp, Joe Lonsdale, Stephen Cohen and Nathan Gettings. There is no earlier partnership, so the incorporation is the earliest formal founding. Note that the company barely operated in its first year - most narrative accounts say Palantir 'started' in 2004, when Thiel and his fund began bankrolling roughly $30M of development, and the S-1's own business section says only 'founded in 2003'. Clocking from 2003-05-06 makes Palantir 17.4 years old at its direct listing, the longest private run in this dataset.

notes.0: The first valuation anyone put on Palantir: $400M in February 2008, from TechCrunch's reconstruction. No lead investor is named in any source loaded here, so `institutional` is left unset rather than asserted - the schema's mechanical test is a NAMED lead, and there isn't one. The round is institutional in substance and sits well after the floor was cleared in 2005-2006, so nothing about the series depends on the flag. Single-source valuation, hence soft.
notes.1: DATED FROM THE FILING, NOT THE PRESS. TechCrunch's table puts this round at June 2010; the Form D says the date of first sale was 2009-11-17, and the June 2010 date is when Palantir filed the amendment (0001321655-10-000001) closing the offering out at $90,058,503 - eight months after the first money moved. The original Form D (0001321655-09-000004, filed 2009-11-30) already showed $34,989,261 sold. The $730M post-money is TechCrunch's single-source figure and is soft; other retellings say $735M. Probably the S-1's Series D (118,957,869 shares at $0.80, liquidation preference $95,166K).
notes.2: Form D date of first sale 2011-04-20, $50,000,000 sold (accession 0001321655-11-000002); TechCrunch dates the same round to May 2011, which is its filing date, and reports the $1.7B post-money. No lead named in any source loaded, so `institutional` is left unset.
notes.3: Form D date of first sale 2011-08-23, $68,000,000 sold (accession 0001321655-11-000003); TechCrunch dates it October 2011 and reports $2.5B post-money. The amount matches the S-1's Series F exactly (34,686,278 shares at $1.98, liquidation preference $68,679K). No lead named, so `institutional` is left unset.
notes.4: Form D date of first sale 2013-09-12, $196,500,204 sold (accession 0001321655-13-000002) - matching the S-1's Series J to within a rounding error (22,055,682 shares at $8.89, liquidation preference $196,075K). TechCrunch reports roughly $6B post-money; Wikipedia instead describes a December 2013 round of about $450M at $9B, which is the NEXT offering (below), not this one. Single-source valuation, soft. No lead named.
notes.5: ONE OFFERING, FOUR FILINGS, AND TWO PHANTOM 'ROUNDS' IN THE PRESS. The Form D series 0001321655-13-000003 / -13-000005 / -14-000002 / -14-000003 all carry the same date of first sale, 2013-11-20, and walk the amount sold up from $57.5M to $177.5M to $279.1M and finally to $444,184,042 in the September 2014 amendment. TechCrunch's table reads those amendments as separate rounds in February 2014 ($111.3M) and September 2014 ($444.2M); they are the same offering. Wikipedia describes a December 2013 raise of about $450M at a $9B valuation, which fits this offering's start and final size, and that is where the $9B comes from. Single-source valuation, soft. No lead named.
notes.6: Form D date of first sale 2014-11-26, $50,000,001 sold (accession 0001321655-14-000005). The $15B mark is carried independently by TechCrunch (which dates it December 2014), by Wikipedia (November 2014) and by the New York Times' December 2015 report that Palantir was 'valued at about $20 billion, up from $15 billion' - three independent statements of the same figure, so confirmed. No lead named.
notes.7: PALANTIR'S PRIVATE PEAK. Form D date of first sale 2015-07-08; the original filing (0001321655-15-000001) showed $450.0M sold against a $500M offering, and the December amendment (0001321655-15-000004) closed it at $879,829,998. TechCrunch broke the final figure on 2015-12-23 from that filing and put the valuation at $20.33B, noting $679.8M had already been raised in the same offering since July; CNBC, Reuters and the New York Times all reported $880M at about $20B the same week, so the figure is confirmed. This is the S-1's Series K (79,009,569 shares at $11.38, liquidation preference $899,130K - the extra $20M is the November 2016 top-up below). Kortschak Investments is named as the investor of record on the filing coverage.
notes.8: DOWN ROUND, AND A REAL ONE: from $20.33B in 2015 to roughly $7B in 2020, a five-year 65% decline in what Palantir could sell equity at. The mechanism is visible in the price per share alone, with no valuation arithmetic involved at all: $11.38 for the 2015 Series K, $6.03 for the 2018 and 2019 Class A sales, $4.65 here. Wikipedia records that Morgan Stanley marked its Palantir position at a roughly $6B company value in 2018, which is consistent. The round itself is documented twice over - Form D 0001321655-20-000001 gives a date of first sale of 2020-04-07 and $549,727,437 sold against a $961,099,010 offering as of 2020-07-01, and the S-1 completes it: "From April 2020 through July 2020, we sold an aggregate of 206,500,523 shares of our Class A common stock to 59 accredited investors at a purchase price of $4.65 per share, for an aggregate purchase price of $960.2 million." THE VALUATION IS AN ESTIMATE AND THE HEURISTIC IS THIS: $4.65 x 1,531,997,752 as-converted shares outstanding at 2020-06-30, both numbers taken from the S-1 (the share count from its Sale Price History of Our Capital Stock table). That is deliberately the same basis the public series uses - shares outstanding, not fully diluted - so the private point and the first market-cap quote are measuring the same thing. It is a floor: roughly a billion options and RSUs are excluded. For comparison, CNBC computed about $7.8B for the July tranche at $4.75 a share and headlined about $10.5B for the company ahead of the listing on a fully diluted basis; that article could not be loaded (HTTP 403) so its figures are not used as the recorded value. No lead named - 59 buyers, of whom Sompo Holdings and Fujitsu were reported participants.

Snowflake builds clean on its own (`--only snowflake`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, cross-check worst 2.65%, regression 0.00%). This is a pipeline ordering artefact, not a data problem in either shard.

companies.curatorNotes: Dropbox has no usable cover-page share tag, so every quarterly point in the public series is computed from a weighted average and is correctly drawn hollow. dei:EntityCommonStockSharesOutstanding and us-gaap:CommonStockSharesOutstanding are both absent from its XBRL facts — it is a Class A/Class B filer and tags the cover count with a share-class axis the companyfacts API does not expose — and us-gaap:CommonStockSharesIssued carries only two non-dimensional values (2020 and 2021). The cascade lands on us-gaap:WeightedAverageNumberOfSharesOutstandingBasic, which holds 22 rows. Two structural gaps follow. First, there is no Q4 row at all: the 10-K reports a full-year weighted average, which the >100-day span filter correctly drops, so every 31 December point is priced on the Q3 average, roughly 85 days stale. Second, Dropbox's 2018 and 2019 10-Qs tagged the figure as WeightedAverageNumberOfShareOutstandingBasicAndDiluted, so the Basic series only begins with the 2019 periods carried as comparatives in the 2020 10-Qs; the six quarters from 2018-06-30 to 2019-09-30 have no share row within 200 days and drop out, leaving 2018 covered only by companiesmarketcap's annual point and by the IPO event itself. The cross-check still passes comfortably: seven overlapping years, worst 2.69% (2024), and 0.28-1.45% everywhere else. What that agreement hides is that companiesmarketcap carries the same lag. Hand-derived truth at 2025-12-31, from the FY2025 10-K, is 167.2M Class A plus 75.7M Class B issued and outstanding plus the 8.3M legally outstanding but unvested co-founder restricted stock awards the balance sheet excludes and the cover page includes — 251.2M shares at the $27.80 close, or $6.98B. The pipeline's 261.1M Q3 average gives $7.26B (3.9% high) and companiesmarketcap gives $7.32B (4.9% high). Dropbox retired about 18% of its stock during 2025, so a one-quarter-stale count costs several per cent there while costing well under one per cent in the flatter years. Excluded events: the March 2017 $600M revolving credit facility is debt, not equity; the third-party tender offer that ran somewhere between 2014 and 2017 (8,193,202 Class A shares issued on conversion, per the S-1) has no disclosed price or date and cannot be turned into a valuation.

TPG Growth participated; David Drummond and David Bonderman joined the board. The Series E ultimately reached 84,140,000 shares at $33.31758 — $2,803 million — across the December 2014 close, the February 2015 extension and the strategic investors (Baidu among them) that followed.

The Series G kept selling at that same price through February 2019 and reached $6,858 million in total — the biggest single line in Uber's cap table — so this event is the first close of a round that never really shut. The $62.5 billion is soft: TechCrunch was relaying a Bloomberg report of a raise in progress, not a company statement. It is corroborated six months later, when TechCrunch describes the Saudi investment as not increasing 'the company's current $62.5 billion value'. No lead is named: the S-1 lists only 'seventy-seven accredited investors' and the December 2015 coverage names none, so asserting one would be recall rather than research.
notes.5: Uber announced the investment itself and TechCrunch reports it 'doesn't increase the company's current $62.5 billion value' — flat to the December 2015 Series G price, which is exactly what the cap table shows: the S-1 records June 2016 sales of 73,812,498 Series G shares at the unchanged $48.772228 to two accredited investors for $3,599,999,981.71, i.e. PIF's $3.5 billion plus roughly $100 million alongside. Yasir Al Rumayyan took a board seat. The largest single cheque written into a private technology company at the time.
notes.6: DOWN MARK, and a real one: the SoftBank consortium bought roughly a 14% stake from existing shareholders at $32.97 per share — the price is in Uber's own S-1 — against the $48.772228 the same consortium paid the company three weeks later. TechCrunch: 'The shares purchased from existing shareholders will value the company at approximately $48 billion, a significant discount to the roughly $69 billion that company was valued at in its last private round.' No money reached Uber, so amountRaisedUsd is null; this is a secondary purchase, and it is plotted because it is a company-run tender at a stated price rather than a platform's indicative mark. The discount is not a re-pricing of the company so much as the price of liquidity after the 2017 governance crisis: Benchmark, Menlo, employees and Travis Kalanick (about 29% of his stake) were the sellers, and Benchmark dropped its lawsuit against Kalanick as part of the deal. Dated to the tender's close (2017-12-28); the overall transaction completed 2018-01-18.
notes.7: The other half of the SoftBank deal, and the reason the tender above is so striking: the consortium put $1.25 billion of new money into the company at $48.772228 per share — the S-1 records 25,629,340 Series G-1 shares sold to sixty-one accredited investors in January 2018 for $1,250,000,013.97, the same price as the Series G. TechCrunch puts the primary at 'the $69 billion value'; other coverage of the same transaction says $68 billion or $70 billion, none of which could be verified here, so the figure is soft. Uber confirmed the close on 2018-01-18, along with the governance changes and SoftBank's board seats.

companies.curatorNotes: Uber's S-1 is the best pre-IPO disclosure in this dataset. Its preferred-stock note gives an issue price for every series (Seed $0.00906, A $0.09248, B $0.35448, C-1 $4.45438, C-2 $3.56350, C-3 $4.45438, D $15.51305, E $33.31758, F $39.638581, G and G-1 $48.772228) and its Item 15 lists twenty-five individual sales, month by month, from September 2015 to February 2019 — which is how the June 2016 Saudi cheque, the January 2018 SoftBank primary and the unattributed October 2018 $500 million can be pinned to the dollar. Round dates are Form D dates of first sale where EDGAR has one (Series B, Series C) and announcement or S-1 dates otherwise; EDGAR holds no Uber Form D before 2012, which is why the 2010 seed and the 2011 Series A rest on press and on the cap table. Two structural facts about the series letters: the press 'Series C' is three charter series (C-1, C-2, C-3) at two different prices, and the 'Series G' is not a round at all but a three-year, $6.9 billion rolling issuance at one fixed price, of which the December 2015 first close and the June 2016 PIF cheque are recorded separately here. The January 2018 SoftBank transaction is deliberately split into two events because it was two transactions at two prices on the same terms sheet — a secondary tender at $32.97 (~$48 billion) and a primary at $48.772228 (~$69 billion) — and collapsing them into one number would erase the most instructive data point in Uber's private history. The $1.15 billion leveraged loan of July 2016 and the 2016/2018 senior notes are debt and are excluded. On the public side: crossCheckTolPct is raised from the default 3.0 to 6.0 for one specific reason, which is a companiesmarketcap error rather than a pipeline one. companiesmarketcap puts Uber's 2020 year-end market cap at $89.95 billion, which at the $51.00 close implies 1,763,768,098 shares — exactly the count on the Q3 2020 cover page, filed six weeks before the Postmates acquisition closed. Uber's own balance sheet says 1,849,794,000 shares were outstanding on 2020-12-31, giving $94.3 billion; the pipeline computes $94.8 billion. The computed series is right and the reference is stale, so the ceiling is raised rather than the data bent. Every other year agrees to within 2.2%.

companies.curatorNotes: Square's 2015 S-1 is close to an ideal source: the preferred-stock note gives shares outstanding, aggregate proceeds and issue price for all six series, the related-party section dates Series D and E, and Exhibit 3.1 supplies both the exact Delaware incorporation date and the original corporate name (Seashell, Inc.). What the S-1 does not give is a post-money valuation for any round, so every valuationUsd here is a press figure and none was ever confirmed by the company. Four Form D filings from 2011 supply exact first-sale dates for the Series B and C, which no secondary source has. Identifiers were verified rather than recalled: SEC's company_tickers.json maps CIK 1512673 to XYZ (SQ returns HTTP 400 from stockanalysis.com and XYZ returns a full quarterly history), and companiesmarketcap still serves Block under the /square/ slug — /block/ 302s to a 404 — with the page itself titled 'Block (XYZ) - Market capitalization'. The public series carries one real defect and the build does not currently pass because of it. dei:EntityCommonStockSharesOutstanding and us-gaap:CommonStockSharesOutstanding are both absent from Block's companyfacts, so the cascade lands on us-gaap:WeightedAverageNumberOfSharesOutstandingBasic and every computed point is marked soft, which is the expected multi-class-filer behaviour. Nine of the ten cross-check years are fine on that tag: 2017 -1.18%, 2018 -1.75%, 2019 -1.29%, 2020 -2.57%, 2021 -0.92%, 2022 -0.90%, 2023 -0.46%, 2024 -0.51%, 2025 -1.66%, all consistent with a weighted average sitting a little under period-end. 2016 is not: it computes -56.65% against companiesmarketcap, and it also trips the continuity check with a 3.05x jump into 2017Q1. The cause is specific rather than general. A weighted-average fact is dated by its filing date, and the CY2015Q3 fact has only one filing — the Q3 2016 10-Q of 2016-11-02, where it appears as the prior-year comparative. So the 2016-12-31 quarter is priced against 152,334,000 shares, which is Square's weighted-average COMMON count for the quarter before it went public and excludes all 135M convertible preferred shares, instead of the roughly 344M shares actually outstanding at the end of 2016. No shard field can reach this: pinning sharesTag to the only other available tag yields four data points and disables the share series entirely, and annualOverrides cannot help because computed quarterly points overwrite overrides in the same quarter. The two fixes both live in build_data.py — either exclude a weighted-average fact whose filing date is more than ~six months after its period end, or restrict nearest_share_row to counts at or before the quarter end (this second one also brings 2020 from -2.57% to under 1%). The regression checkpoint below was deliberately left at companiesmarketcap's independent 2024 figure of $52.66B rather than tuned to the pipeline's output; the pipeline reproduces it at $52.39B, 0.51% low, hand-checked as the 2024Q4 close of $84.99 times the 616,428,000 shares in the CY2024Q3 fact filed 2024-11-07.

companies.curatorNotes: Stripe is the rare private company with a near-complete public valuation history — 11 of 12 priced rounds carry a reported number, far above the usual one-in-five — because it is large enough that every round is a news event and because since 2024 it has published its own tender prices. SEC Form D is the backbone of the amounts. Stripe's EDGAR history begins in November 2016 (CIK 0001691342) and no Form D exists for any earlier round; from 2016 onward every Form D amount matches or slightly exceeds the announced figure. Four small Form Ds are not recorded as rounds because they have no lead, no valuation and no press coverage, and are most likely acquisition consideration or option-related issuances: first sale 2017-03-15 ($5,050,010 of $5,300,017 offered), 2017-07-19 ($6,215,086), 2018-03-02 ($38,652,942) and 2019-08-27 ($2,000,013). Deliberately excluded: secondary-market platform marks, including Nasdaq Private Market's $67.26/share estimate as of 2026-06-01, which have no disclosed share count and cannot be converted to a company valuation. Also excluded is the July 2022 (~$74B) and January 2023 (~$63B) internal 409A sequence, which Contrary reports but which are appraisals rather than transactions. Stripe has never filed an S-1 and has never IPO'd; as of 2026-08-06 that is still true, with John Collison telling Davos in January 2026 that going public 'isn't one of our top five or ten or twenty priorities'. Stripe's own reported $53B bid for PayPal in 2026 is a use of its equity, not a mark on it, and is not recorded here.

Series A through D disclosed no valuation at all and are plot:false — four of sixteen events. EDGAR also exposes four offerings Databricks never announced: $673,757,396 (first sale 2022-09-30), $1,567,882,333 (2023-11-03), $665,723,223 (2025-05-27) and a small $23,017,200 (first sale 2025-09-30, Form D filed 2025-12-31). Ali Ghodsi told Bloomberg Television that 2026 is 'a terrible year to go public', pointing at 2027 at the earliest, and the July 2026 Coatue round is the company choosing more private capital over a listing. companies.curatorNotes: Opendoor is the clearest 'read the filings, not the headlines' case in this dataset, and the trap runs the opposite way to the expected one. Every Opendoor headline round number - $210M in 2016, $325M in June 2018, $400M from SoftBank, $300M in 2019 - is pure equity, and the enormous debt figures that appear in the same press releases ($400M in 2016, $1.5B in 2018, $2B in late 2018, $3B in 2019) are always cumulative company-level warehouse and mezzanine facilities used to buy houses, stated in separate sentences. The proof is arithmetic: Opendoor published a running equity total with almost every round ($110M, $320M, $645M, $1.045B, $1.3B) and the ladder only closes if every headline is all-equity. DATING POLICY: rounds are dated to the Form D date of first sale where a Form D exists (Series A through D) because that is the day money changed hands, and to the announcement date otherwise (Series E, the SoftBank tranche, Series E-2). Opendoor Labs Inc. (CIK 0001609437) filed exactly seven Form Ds, all between 2014-05-29 and 2016-12-12, and none for the Series E, E-1 or E-2 - so the 2018-2019 rounds exist in the public record only through press releases and the S-4/A audited cap table. AMOUNTS are the announced headline figures with the Form D and audited figures recorded in each note; the two disagree most for the Series C (filed $76.7M against an announced $80M, the balance sold after the unamended filing) and the Series E-2 (announced $300M against an audited $282.9M). VALUATIONS: only two of ten events carry one, both soft and both traceable to a single unnamed TechCrunch source - about $2B for June 2018 and $3.8B for March 2019. Series A through D disclosed nothing at all, and the S-4/A cap table cannot rescue them, because reconstructing a post-money needs the fully diluted count at each round date and the filing does not give it retrospectively; the charter also names Series C-1 and D-1 tranches that never appear as separate balance-sheet lines, leaving 2017 activity invisible (Series D carrying value rose to $223,072K by 2017-12-31, above the $213.4M Series D offering). GOING PUBLIC: publicFrom is the de-SPAC completion date 2020-12-18, not the start of the price history. stockanalysis.com's OPEN series reaches back to 2020-06 because the ticker inherited the SPAC shell's quotes - the Q3 2020 point at $18.99 is a blank-cheque vehicle with no operating business, and gating on 2020-12-18 removes it, so the first public point is 2020-12-31. The CIK is the SPAC's, carried forward: EDGAR shows 0001801169 as Social Capital Hedosophia Holdings Corp. II until 2020-12-18 and Opendoor Technologies Inc. after. SHARE COUNT: sharesTag is pinned to the us-gaap balance-sheet instant CommonStockSharesOutstanding rather than the default dei cover-page count. The cover page is printed six to eight weeks after quarter end and Opendoor dilutes fast enough that this matters - the FY2020 cover count of 577,227,618 (as of 2021-02-26, after a wave of warrant exercises) overstates the 2020-12-31 market cap by 6.7% against the balance-sheet 540,714,692, and the FY2025 cover count is 958,325,481 against a 2025-12-31 balance of 957,245,487. CROSS-CHECK CEILING: crossCheckTolPct is raised from the default 3.0 to 3.5 for one specific, documented reason. With the balance-sheet tag the computed series agrees with companiesmarketcap to 0.6% in 2020, 0.6% in 2021, 1.3% in 2022, 1.2% in 2023 and 2.6% in 2025, but reads 3.2% low in 2024 - because companiesmarketcap's $1.19B for 2024 implies about 746M shares against the 719,990,121 Opendoor actually reported on its FY2024 balance sheet and the 723,517,956 on the 10-K cover. This is drift in the oracle's share count on a company that issues stock continuously, not a structural failure: a wrong tag or a missed split lands at 4x or 40%, never at 3.2%. Nor is it fixable by switching tags. The dei cover-page count would pull 2024 in at 2.7% but push 2020 out to 6.1%, because it is printed 57 days after the year end and after a wave of warrant exercises; no available share tag clears 3.0% at both ends. Post-listing the story is a ~95% drawdown and a violent recovery: about $12.3B at the end of 2020, $9.0B end-2021, $739M end-2022 (a 94% fall as the iBuyer model met rising rates and Opendoor wrote down inventory), $3.0B end-2023, $1.15B end-2024, a low of $391M at 2025-06-30, then a meme-driven rally to $6.1B by 2025-09-30 and $5.6B at end-2025, and roughly $3.3B today (2026-08-06: a $3.445 close on 968,626,958 shares). The 2025-06-30 to 2025-09-30 move is a genuine 15.7x quarter, not a missed split - the share series is continuous and Opendoor has never split.

companies.foundedNote: OpenAI, Inc. was incorporated in Delaware as a non-stock, non-profit corporation on 2015-12-08 — the Certificate of Incorporation is reproduced as an exhibit to Musk v. On 2025-10-28 the capped-profit arm was recapitalised into OpenAI Group PBC, a Delaware public benefit corporation with ordinary equity, still controlled by the renamed OpenAI Foundation; Delaware's Attorney General completed her review the same day and did not object.

companies.curatorNotes: OpenAI is the hardest 'post-money' in this dataset, because for most of its life it had no ordinary equity. From March 2019 to October 2025 investors bought capped-profit units in OpenAI LP (later OpenAI Global, LLC) whose returns were contractually capped — 100x for the 2019 cohort, lower for later ones — and Microsoft's three investments in particular were structured as a profit waterfall (reportedly 75% of profits until recoupment, then a 49% economic interest) rather than as preferred stock. None of Microsoft's investments in 2019, 2021 or January 2023 ever carried a disclosed post-money, and the widely repeated '$29 billion valuation' attached to the January 2023 deal is a report of what Microsoft was 'looking to' pay, not a priced round; all three are therefore recorded with valuationUsd: null and left off the line. On 2025-10-28 the capped-profit arm was recapitalised into OpenAI Group PBC, a Delaware public benefit corporation with real equity, controlled by the OpenAI Foundation (26%); Microsoft's converted stake was ~27%, worth about $135B, with employees and other investors holding ~47%. Delaware's Attorney General completed her review and declined to object the same day. Four of the seven plotted points are tender-offer prices rather than primary rounds (2021, April 2023, February 2024, October 2025); all are marked tender/soft and render hollow, because a price at which employees sold to funds is not a negotiated primary post-money. companies.curatorNotes:
IPO status as of 2026-08-06: Anthropic, PBC confidentially submitted a draft Form S-1 to the SEC on 2026-06-01 and said the submission 'gives us the option to go public after the SEC completes its review', with share count and price not yet set. Nothing is public on EDGAR (confidential submissions are not published), no public S-1 exists, no underwriters have been formally announced, and no shares have priced. Anthropic is therefore still private and status stays 'private'. Reporting of an October 2026 Nasdaq listing with Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley leading appears only on low-quality IPO-tracker sites; Fortune says those banks are 'expected to be under consideration' with no formal appointments. Treat any IPO date, size or listing valuation as unsourced.

Structure: Amazon's and Google's money is genuinely different from the lettered rounds. Amazon's first $8B (Sept 2023, Mar 2024, Nov 2024) was convertible notes tied to an AWS cloud-and-chips commercial agreement, confirmed by Amazon's own 10-Qs rather than by either party's press release; those notes converted to nonvoting preferred in tranches during Q1 2025 and Q1 2026, and $42.2B of notes were still outstanding at 2026-03-31. Only the April 2026 $5B was straight preferred stock, and even there the contingent $20B facility draws as new convertible notes. Google's tranches (Feb 2023, Oct 2023, Jan 2025, Apr 2026) were never characterised as notes by any source and are recorded as equity investments, each tied to a cloud-compute commitment. None of the six hyperscaler events carries a disclosed conversion price, which is why they are all valuationUsd null and unplotted — five of the eight unplotted events in this file.

Plotting decisions worth defending: seven of the nineteen events are plotted. The two April 2026 marks at $350B (the employee tender and Google's $10B) are recorded with their prices but not plotted, because $350B is the February Series G's pre-money — the same per-share price already represented by the $380B post-money vertex — and plotting it would draw a down round that did not occur. This is a deliberate departure from the default that company-run tender offers are plottable.

Valuation provenance: the first five events (2021-2023, through SK Telecom) have no defensible valuation at all. PitchBook's and Forge's $623M Series A post-money has no primary support and is excluded. The curve therefore starts at the Series C. The Series C ($4.1B) and Series D ($18.4B) are soft — both trace to single-outlet reporting on pitch decks and talks rather than to closed prices, and Anthropic confirmed neither. Everything from the Series E onward is company-confirmed post-money from Anthropic's own posts.

Revenue for context (all Anthropic-disclosed): ~$1B run-rate January 2025, over $5B August 2025, ~$9B end-2025, $14B February 2026, over $30B April 2026, over $47B May 2026. Claude Code alone passed $2.5B run-rate by February 2026.

Excluded: secondary-market platform marks. Coverage of the April 2026 tender noted secondary pricing implying $500B-$800B, but these are indicative platform quotes with no disclosed share count and cannot be converted to a company valuation. Also excluded: Anthropic's compute and infrastructure partnerships that carry no investment (the April 2026 Google/Broadcom TPU expansion, the reported Meta compute-leasing talks).

Disclosure: this file was researched by Claude, made by Anthropic. It was held to the same evidence standard as the rest of the dataset — every figure is either from a fetched primary filing, a fetched company post, or fetched press, and unconfirmed numbers are marked soft. Nothing here rests on the researcher's familiarity with the subject.

The $80B is therefore an exchange ratio set by a controlling holder on both sides, not a price an outside investor paid. The key fact: $75.46 is exactly xAI's Series E issue price, so the merger did not reprice xAI. The line ends at the Series E, the last priced round before the merger, and SpaceX's own shard carries the story from there.
